title: Prioritize Narrative as the leading candidate for a controlled intervention to preserve a company‑first framing
description: The experiments show Narrative is the most recurrent first‑visible stage where company‑first hierarchy breaks and unsupported claims appear; treat Narrative as the primary candidate for a focused gate or controlled trial rather than as a proven single cause. Design and test a Narrative‑focused control while explicitly acknowledging that Idea or Synthesis have been first‑visible origins in some runs and therefore must remain in scope if the trial shows remaining failures.
audience: Prompt engineers, editorial leads, experiment designers, and product owners responsible for Nuëyon.Compose pipeline quality and gating.
rationale: Why it matters: The report identifies Narrative as the most common first-visible locus of hierarchy drift across multiple runs (Experiments 007–009). Because Narrative shapes the reader-facing through-line, a controlled Narrative-focused intervention is a plausible, evidence-aligned place to start. Caveats and uncertainty: The source explicitly cautions that Narrative is not the sole origin—some runs show Idea or Synthesis as first drift—so a Narrative-only fix is not assumed sufficient. The recommended approach is a controlled upstream-boundary trial that tests whether a Narrative gate preserves the intended company-first → product-as-support relationship; if drift persists, examine Idea and Synthesis next. This recommendation follows the report’s own phrasing: it “is a diagnostic recommendation, not a prompt rewrite.”
evidence: Report assertion: “Narrative is the most recurrent first visible hierarchy shift in the available records.” Localized examples: Experiment 007 — Narrative first in candidate 001–002; Experiment 008 A-002 — Narrative invents founders and product leads; Experiment 009 — Narrative identified as first clear editorial shift in baseline 002/003 and candidates 001–003. Counterexamples noted: 007 candidate 003 shifts at Synthesis; several Experiment 008 runs show Idea-origin drift. Report recommendation: run a controlled trial targeting Narrative (Implication for the next focused trial, point 1 and following).

title: Remove upstream format references to close an instruction‑boundary inconsistency that plausibly primes downstream framing
description: Upstream prompts (Idea/Research/Narrative) contain explicit references to formats and article‑writing roles despite the Master Workflow’s format‑independence rule. Treat these references as an architectural inconsistency to be corrected or isolated and test whether removing them reduces format‑primed story selection before Compose.
audience: Prompt architects, workflow designers, and governance teams managing prompt boundaries and prompt-library hygiene in Nuëyon.Compose.
rationale: Why it matters: If upstream agents are unintentionally primed to optimize for LinkedIn or article mechanics, their story selection may be shaped by presentation concerns rather than by the intended company-first editorial hierarchy. The report calls this an instruction‑boundary inconsistency and highlights plausible priming while explicitly noting it does not prove causation. Gaps and uncertainty: The report describes the leakage and calls it plausible source of priming but recommends a controlled trial to validate causation; removing format references should be tested in isolation or as a controlled condition to avoid confounding other changes.
evidence: Observed prompt content: “Frozen Idea system prompt includes ‘supported output formats’”; Research system prompt lists “an article writer” in role exclusions; Narrative system prompt names articles, LinkedIn posts, newsletters and requires story direction to work for “both Article and LinkedIn formats.” Master Workflow states upstream stages should remain format-independent; report labels these upstream format references an architectural inconsistency and a plausible source of priming (Format-agnostic architecture audit).

title: Split evaluation into separate factual‑fidelity and editorial‑quality gates to catch distinct failure modes
description: Introduce parallel evaluation tracks: (a) strict factual/source-fidelity checks (claims, audience, certainty) and (b) editorial-quality measurements (opening hook, clarity, narrative progression, readable phrasing). Use both gates to accept an output only when it passes factual integrity and editorial effectiveness criteria.
audience: QA teams, annotation/evaluation designers, editorial reviewers, and product managers responsible for Compose evaluation metrics and acceptance criteria.
rationale: Why it matters: The report documents that factual errors and editorial weaknesses are distinct: source‑aligned but dull or poorly framed outputs still fail the company‑first purpose, while engaging language can introduce unsupported claims. Current evaluations focused mainly on factuality and hierarchy and under‑measured engagement. Gaps and uncertainty: The report does not prescribe a validated editorial rubric; creating and calibrating reliable editorial metrics will require human-judged trials and inter-rater agreement. Implementing parallel gates means defining pass/fail thresholds and validating them against downstream Compose amplification behaviors.
evidence: Report statements: “Factual and editorial failures are distinct.” “The artifact evaluations did not apply a consistent hook/readability/attention rubric to every run, so this observation is qualitative.” Recommendation: separately evaluate (a) factual claims/audience/certainty, (b) company-first story hierarchy, and (c) editorial quality (opening interest, clarity, narrative progression, concise readable prose).

title: Frame a controlled upstream‑boundary experiment (Narrative‑first trial) that replicates the report’s recommended design
description: Convert the report’s five-point diagnostic recommendation into a reproducible experimental brief: target Narrative as the primary tested locus, enforce a rule preserving company-as-subject with Compose as supporting product direction, keep prompts constant except for the tested Narrative changes, run repeated full‑pipeline interleaved trials, and evaluate three separate dimensions (factual fidelity, hierarchy, editorial quality).
audience: Experiment leads, research coordinators, and product managers who will run and analyze Nuëyon.Compose trials.
rationale: Why it matters: The report itself recommends this precise controlled trial as the next step to determine whether Narrative‑level controls reduce downstream reframing and unsupported claims. Translating that recommendation into a concrete experiment design reduces ambiguity and enables reproducible assessment. Gaps and uncertainty: The report frames this as a recommendation to be executed; it does not claim results. The brief should include exact prompts, pass/fail criteria, data-capture requirements, and pre‑registered analysis plans to avoid post-hoc interpretation.
evidence: Report section “Implication for the next focused trial” lists five explicit trial requirements: (1) target Narrative (most recurrent locus), (2) test rule to preserve company-level subject and product-as-support, (3) avoid removing output-format reasoning unless hypothesis targets leakage, (4) run repeated full-pipeline runs with capture and interleaving, (5) separately evaluate factual/audience/certainty, company-first hierarchy, and editorial quality. The report reiterates: “This is a diagnostic recommendation, not a prompt rewrite.”

title: Constrain Compose’s tendency to amplify upstream framing by adding final‑stage factuality limits and conservative language rules
description: Because Compose sometimes strengthens or adds factual claims that exceed upstream support (e.g., ‘orchestration‑first’, ‘reliably converts’), add Compose-specific constraints: conservative claim language, explicit source‑claim linking, and a final factual‑assertion checklist to prevent amplification beyond the source evidence.
audience: Compose output engineers, content reviewers, and product managers responsible for final-stage output policies and safeguards.
rationale: Why it matters: Even when upstream story selection is correct, Compose can magnify claims into stronger, unsupported statements. Adding final-stage constraints reduces risk of amplifying unsupported language and complements upstream controls. Gaps and uncertainty: The report provides examples of Compose amplifications but does not quantify relative frequency; such Compose constraints should be piloted and measured alongside upstream trials to determine marginal benefit and avoid over‑constraining legitimate narrative clarity.
evidence: Report examples and wording: Compose escalations include phrases like “orchestration-first,” “reliably converts,” and “predictable and repeatable.” Report observation: “Compose can amplify, add factual strength, or simply inherit,” and gives multiple runs where Compose strengthens upstream frames into stronger claims.
